### MFA and Just-in-Time Provisioning: Tighter DAM Security Without Slowing Users Down

Enterprise DAM platforms support both multi-factor authentication (MFA) and just-in-time (JIT) provisioning, usually through single sign-on (SSO) with your company’s identity provider. MFA adds a second check at login, and JIT provisioning creates a user’s account and permissions automatically the first time they sign in. Many enterprises also use SCIM, which keeps DAM accounts in sync with the company directory and removes access when someone leaves.

### Polymorphic DAM: What Darwin’s Finches Teach Us About Enterprise Content

Quick Takeaways A polymorphic DAM gives each department its own version of the platform, with an interface and workflows built for that team, while everyone works from one shared asset repository. The idea comes from biology. Darwin's finches developed different beaks for different environments but stayed finches. One-size-fits-all DAMs struggle with adoption, and best-in-breed DAMs create silos. A polymorphic DAM avoids that tradeoff. Common configurations include a marketing DAM, a video MAM, and a corporate archive, all running on the same system.

[Read More](https://www.orangelogic.com/dam-blog/what-is-a-polymorphic-dam)

### Open the Door, Not the Vault: Managing Agency and Partner Access to Your DAM Securely

Quick Takeaways To securely manage agency and partner access, provide a customized portal with access only to the assets they need. Limit permissions to what each engagement requires, from review-only roles to rights-aware visibility. Review partner downloads and remove inactive accounts each quarter. Most content teams field requests from outside the building every week. A creative agency needs approved photography for a campaign, an international distributor wants localized video for its markets, and a journalist is waiting on press images ahead of a deadline. Each of them works with you, and each needs a very different slice of the library. Over time, those views tend to pile up. Logins created for a single campaign stay active long after it wraps, and file sharing links sent in a hurry keep working for anyone they get forwarded to. After a few dozen campaigns, it gets hard to say who still has access to what, and if the assets shared are still the right ones for each audience. That gap matters more every year. Verizon's2025 Data Breach Investigations Report found third parties were involved in 30% of breaches, up from about 15% the year before. The sections below walk through how to give partners what they need while keeping a clear record of who can reach what. What Are the Risks of Giving Agencies DAM Access? Every outside login is another way into your library, and each one carries compliance weight. In aForrester Consulting study commissioned by Orange Logic, 64% of the 313 DAM decision-makers surveyed said they face legal and regulatory compliance challenges with their digital assets. Permissions are a big part of that. More than half of respondents (56%) said they find it hard to set permissions that let more people use rich-media assets safely. When asked which DAM capabilities will matter most two years from now, more of them picked expanded digital rights management than anything else (44%). What Permissions Should External Partners Have to your DAM? Permissions for outside users work best when they follow the scope of the engagement. Separate workspaces. Give agencies and partners their own space with their own set of permissions. Group-level access. Assign permissions to the agency as a group so new team members inherit the correct access when they join. Review-only roles. Give stakeholders who only approve work a preview without download rights. Rights-aware visibility. Hide assets with expired licenses or regional restrictions from partners who can't use them. Single sign-on. Require SSO or multi-factor authentication on every external account. With permissions mapped to the engagement, a new agency can start on day one without anyone on your team assembling folders by hand. Share Links That Expire on Their Own Plenty of partner requests are one-off, like a photographer pulling selects or a retailer grabbing launch imagery. A link that expires after a set date keeps a single share from turning into permanent access. Expiring links work for single assets, folders, or whole collections. User-specific watermarks add a visible deterrent, since each downloaded copy is marked with details tied to the person who requested it. Invisible watermarks go a step further, helping trace a leaked file back to its source even after it's been cropped or reposted. When a contract ends, deactivate the agency's accounts the same day and revoke access for any sharing links. How Do You Track What Partners Download? An activity report shows which assets each partner downloaded and when, which is usually the first thing you'll want to check if something turns up where it shouldn't. Plenty of teams wish they had more of that visibility. In Orange Logic’s commissioned Forrester study, 68% of leaders said they need a better understanding of how their assets are used and how they perform. The same reports can show how quickly each agency moves work through approvals, which comes in handy going into a contract renewal. It also helps to set a quarterly reminder to clean house, removing accounts that haven't logged in for a while and closing workspaces for projects that have wrapped. How Does Orange Logic Handle Partner Access? Each practice above has a matching feature in Orange Logic, built for teams that work with several agencies and partners at once. Siloed agency portals. Give your larger agencies a portal that hides other agencies' uploads and comments, then track approvals for all of them from one dashboard. Branded Spaces. Set up a hub for each partner with its own permissions and look, while every asset still comes from the same central library. Group and time-bound permissions. Assign access by group, set permissions to expire on a date, and connect external accounts to single sign-on or multi-factor authentication. Expiring links and watermarks. Share assets, folders, or collections through links that shut off on schedule, and add user-specific watermarks to downloaded copies. An integration with IMATAG adds invisible, traceable watermarks for identifying the source of an unauthorized release. Agency reporting. Measure how efficiently each agency moves work through review, and bring that data to your next contract conversation. Since every portal and Space pulls from the same library, partners always work from the approved version of an asset. Case Studies: How Lionsgate and PMC Share Assets With Partners Media companies run into partner access questions constantly, since trailers, key art, and talent images pass through studios, agencies, and distributors long before anything goes public. Two Orange Logic customers show what this looks like at scale. Lionsgate moved its marketing teams onto Orange Logic as the single home for final, approved assets, replacing seven separate storage locations. More than 800 global partners, including agencies, distributors, and streaming platforms, now get self-service access to production-ready content. When a partner receives a share, they pick the file version they need, since Orange Logic generates derivative formats on ingest. PMC, the company behind Variety, Billboard, and Rolling Stone, manages more than 9 million assets across 40 brands. Each brand works in its own workspace, with role-based access for internal teams and external partners, a setup built to keep pace with more than 300 live events a year. Where to Start With Partner Access Most teams don't need to rework partner access all at once. A good first step is the outside relationship that already sends the most requests, which is usually a lead agency. Map what that team actually needs to see, set up their workspace and permissions around it, and use what you learn as the template for the partners that follow. Once that first setup is in place, it gets much easier to say who can reach what in your library, and why. ### Can a DAM Store and Govern Approved Copy and Messaging, Not Just Files?

Yes, a digital asset management (DAM) system can store and govern approved copy and messaging, not just files. A DAM treats approved text the way it treats an image or a video. Each piece of copy gets an owner, metadata, an approval state, a version history, access permissions, and an expiration date. Every team, agency, and channel then pulls the current approved wording from one governed source instead of copying it out of old decks and email threads.
